body.text: The second week at Victoria's Big Build royal commission was a colourful one
There is no such thing as a free lunch, except on the Big Build, where the Victorian taxpayer picked up the bill.
This week, the royal commission probing corruption and criminality in Victoria's construction sector tallied up some of the receipts.
It aired evidence of a $20,000 souvlaki scam lunch, $12,000 in donations to the CFMEU and $17,000 worth of fake invoices.
Then there were pay cheques for bikies and union officials worth hundreds of thousands of dollars for work that was never done or explained.

And already, the commission has referred two witnesses to police — understood to be Bandidos bikie Joel Leavitt and BK Labour Hire boss Bernard Kearney — over allegations they failed to answer questions during their evidence.
If prosecuted and proven guilty, they face two years' imprisonment or a fine of $50,000.
'I cannot recall' heard more than 300 times

Commissioner Chris Kourakis AC repeatedly warned both witnesses in the face of their apparent amnesia in the witness box that answering questions by claiming to have no memory of events could constitute an offence.
"Just because words come out of your mouth after a question doesn't mean that you've answered it," Mr Kourakis emphasised to Mr Kearney.
During intense grilling from the commission, Rebels-turned-Bandidos bikie Mr Leavitt said he could not remember what happened for most of 2021 and 2022.
He uttered a variation of "I cannot recall" more than 300 times.
"Have you seen a medical practitioner about your lack of recollection of two years of your life?" the commissioner asked.
"You've not received any diagnosis of cognitive decline or recollection decline?"
"No," Leavitt replied.
The bikie blamed PTSD from having been shot, his ADHD and past drug use for his memory failure, as well as being "slightly hungover" on his second day of evidence.

The commission heard the CFMEU had muscled the bikie onto Big Build sites, as the union's nominated health and safety representative, via his employment by the union's preferred labour hire firm, BK Labour.
The commission heard once Mr Leavitt started getting work on jobs, the bikie dined out on the contractors' dime — with the state ultimately picking up most of the bill.

On one occasion, evidence showed that he, along with a fellow CFMEU-nominated health and safety (HSR) representative, cashed in on a workers' souvlaki lunch, having inflated the bill from $9,000 to $20,000 and pocketed the change.

"The workers would get a few souvlakia, the CFMEU members would get a few souvlakia, and maybe some other things, and their two HSR reps were going to pocket $5,000 each and it looks like you were one of the HSR reps," Commissioner Kourakis said.
"Can I take it you're not surprised that you might have engaged in that conduct?"
Mr Leavitt replied: "I'll accept that I'm not surprised that I could of [sic]."

The commission also aired evidence Mr Leavitt claimed wages for shifts while he was either at the gym or at home and had boasted about costing a Big Build project half a million dollars by causing delays.
Cocaine helped bikie 'zone in' on paperwork

Under questioning, Mr Leavitt said there "was a possibility" he could have controlled who worked on construction sites on behalf of the CFMEU, and had arranged jobs for his fellow bikies and their partners.
The bikie also invoiced the CFMEU's preferred labour hire firm, BK Labour, $165,000 as a consultant but could not recall the detail of that work, except that it involved "tips on safety".
In response, the commissioner asked him if he was good at detailed paperwork, to which the bikie suggested only after "a big line" of cocaine, which allowed him to "zone in".
BK Labour's boss Mr Kearney later conceded he had paid the bikie but he had not done any work, telling the inquiry he "just decided to pay it and move on".
Mr Carr wrapped up a day and a half of questioning of Mr Leavitt with two propositions.

"One conclusion that might be reached is that you were nothing more than a bikie heavy who the CFMEU wanted on building sites so you could intimidate people into doing what the union wanted," he said.
"I wouldn't say that's a conclusion I would reach, but — is that your conclusion?" Mr Leavitt responded.
Mr Carr offered a second option.

"What about this? You took full advantage of the power of the CFMEU to pilfer money, to get your bikie mates jobs, to unlawfully benefit the union, all at the expense of the state; do you say that's a fair conclusion to reach on the basis of what I've put to you over the last day and a half?" Mr Carr said.
Mr Leavitt replied: "Again, counsellor, I wouldn't say that that would be my conclusion."

In its first two weeks, the royal commission focused on the 2022 Gap Road level crossing removal, hearing it was one of the few remaining projects that the CFMEU had gained control of through an enterprise agreement and installing its own health and safety reps.
The inquiry probed why BK Labour Hire began winning lucrative contracts on the state's multi-billion dollar Big Build projects, including at Gap Road.

Witnesses have testified that the CFMEU had insisted the project's contractors, John Holland, engage the labour hire firm after the union stopped work for two days during a critical time on the project.

In a meeting at the CFMEU's headquarters in Melbourne's CBD, contractors capitulated to the union's demands to engage BK Labour and use the union's nominated health and safety reps, in order to end the stoppage and resume works.

Despite being a labour hire firm, BK Labour did not provide the actual labour. instead, the workers "switched shirts", having been forced to resign from Zoom recruitment and work for BK Labour, and sign up to the CFMEU for up to $1,200 a year in fees.
The labour hire firm billed contractors for two non-working CFMEU-nominated health and safety reps for about $2,000 a day on the job, according to a tendered invoice.
'Elaborate forgery' used for fake invoices

Investigating the business's finances, the inquiry heard the firm supplied fake invoices to the labour hire authority when the regulator asked the business to explain why it had paid former CFMEU boss Joe Myles $127,000 and had withdrawn $77,000 in cash.
The invoices totalling $17,000 were faked to suggest the firm had sponsored junior football clubs and a bowling club in Melbourne, by way of explaining the cash withdrawals, the commission heard.
The firm never provided an explanation to the industry regulator about why it had paid the union boss.
At Thursday's hearing when Mr Carr asked Mr Kearney if someone had done some "elaborate forgery to come up with the fake invoices", the witness told the hearing: "It happened, yes."
Quizzed further, Mr Kearney conceded he had asked his office manager to fudge the invoice.
"I'll take the rap for that, yeah" he said.
At first Mr Kearney claimed it was his handwriting on the invoices, but later admitted it was not him, prompting a warning from Mr Kourakis.
"I really want to impress on you the grave legal risks which you are taking … you have just confessed to giving false evidence," the commissioner said.
The regulator cancelled the business's licence after it determined the invoices were fake, and Mr Kearney was fined but not convicted after pleading guilty to falsifying documents.

More account statements and invoices aired at the royal commission showed the firm paid about $12,000 in donations to the CFMEU and related companies, as well as paid a union fine issued by the former Australian Building and Construction Commission.
Sacked union official retained as consultant

The inquiry heard that after the CFMEU's Joe Myles had been sacked by the union's administrator in late 2024, the labour hire firm retained him as a "consultant" because of his expertise in workplace safety.
Over a period of almost 10 months, the firm paid Mr Myles $282,000, according to tendered documents.

Mr Kearney told the hearing he thought with Mr Myles's "knowledge he would be an asset to us because he knows health and safety inside out" but conceded he had never actually seen any of Mr Myles's work.
His co-owner, Duane Allen, added that Mr Myles was engaged to update the firm's "policies and processes", including those on "social inclusion" but had only seen him in the office a handful of times.
He agreed paying that amount of money looked like a "pretty silly business decision".
But Mr Carr said it was "illogical and irrational" for the general manager to be "anything other than outraged" about the eye-watering payments, suggesting they were actually a quid pro quo.
"I don't know what a quid pro quo is, counsel" Mr Allen said.

Mr Carr suggested that when Mr Myles was a senior vice-president of the union, he'd been in the position to give the firms access to the Big Build and after he'd been ousted from the union, had paid him to update "a couple policies".
"What was the quarter of a million bucks actually for?" Mr Carr asked.
"That was for the policies and procedures," Mr Allen said.
The hearings will revisit the relationship between the union and the labour hire firm, and what went wrong on the troubled Gap Road level crossing project, two days after the Victorian election.
